Solving and reading results

Source: vignettes/articles/solving.Rmd
solving.Rmd
library(multimod)

vignette("ast") builds a model in R. This article takes that model to a solution and back: what the model object contains once it has data, where its files go, how multimod turns it into a matrix or into code for another toolchain, how to run that code, how the results come back, and what to look at when two routes disagree. The example is example_models$toy, three technologies supplying two regions. The chunks that need a solver run where it is installed; the text quotes the numbers from a run with all of them present.

The model as an object 

toy <- example_models$toy
toy
#> Model: toy
#> Description: two-region capacity expansion toy model
#> Language:  multimod 
#> Sets:  2 
#> Mappings:  2 
#> Aliases:  0 
#> Parameters:  4 
#> Variables:  3 
#> Equations:  3

A model is a list of named components. Two kinds of content live in it and it pays to keep them apart:

  • Declarations say what exists. A parameter has dimensions, a variable has dimensions and a domain, an equation has sides, a relation and a domain. Rendering to any language only needs declarations.
  • Data says how much of it exists. Sets carry their members, mappings their tuples, parameters their values. Solving needs data.

The domain is the hinge between the two. A variable declared over c("tech", "region") with domain "mTR" has one instance per row of the mapping mTR, not one per combination of the sets. That is how a sparse model stays sparse, and it is also the first thing to check when an equation produces no rows.

toy$variables$vGen$domain
#> [1] "mTR"
nrow(toy$mappings$mTR$data)
#> [1] 6
toy$equations$eqDemand$domain$name
#> [1] "mR"
toy$parameters$pDemand$data
#>   region value
#> 1  north  1000
#> 2  south   600

The workspace

Everything written for a solver goes into one directory, the workspace. Its layout is fixed so that the generated code can find the data and so that results land where multimod expects to read them:

<model_dir>/
  model.rds, metadata.json, format.txt    the structure and the data format
  sets/<name>/data.csv                    one file per set
  mappings/<name>/data.csv                one file per mapping
  parameters/<name>/data.csv              one file per parameter
  solvers/gmpl/   model.mod, data.dat     MathProg, written by write_gmpl()
  solvers/jump/   model.jl,  data.jl      JuMP,     written by write_jump()
  solvers/pyomo/  model.py,  data.py      Pyomo,    written by write_pyomo()
  solvers/<backend>/solution/             what the solver run leaves behind
  variables/<name>/data.csv               solutions loaded back into the model

save_model() creates a workspace explicitly (see “Model workspace and data” for formats and lazy loading). The writers create one themselves when the directory they are given is empty, which is what this article does:

ws <- tempfile("toy-")
dir.create(ws)

Solving in R

The matrix route does not generate code. model_to_lp() walks the equations and the data and assembles the LP arrays directly.

lp <- model_to_lp(toy)
names(lp)
#>  [1] "A"                "obj"              "row_lo"           "row_up"          
#>  [5] "col_lo"           "col_up"           "maximum"          "objective_symbol"
#>  [9] "row_index"        "col_index"        "zeroed"
dim(lp$A)
#> [1]  9 13

Each equation contributes one row per tuple of its domain mapping: six for eqCapLim (every tuple of mTR), two for eqDemand (every region in mR), one for the scalar eqCost. Each variable contributes one column per tuple of its domain: six, six, and one for vCost. The two index tables are the dictionary between matrix positions and model symbols, and every result table is built on them:

lp$row_index
#>        i   symbol     i1     i2  sense   rhs
#>    <int>   <char> <char> <char> <char> <num>
#> 1:     1 eqCapLim   coal  north     <=    NA
#> 2:     2 eqCapLim    gas  north     <=    NA
#> 3:     3 eqCapLim   wind  north     <=    NA
#> 4:     4 eqCapLim   coal  south     <=    NA
#> 5:     5 eqCapLim    gas  south     <=    NA
#> 6:     6 eqCapLim   wind  south     <=    NA
#> 7:     7 eqDemand  north   <NA>     >=    NA
#> 8:     8 eqDemand  south   <NA>     >=    NA
#> 9:     9   eqCost   <NA>   <NA>     ==    NA
lp$col_index[c(1, 7, 13), ]
#>        j symbol     i1     i2    lo    up      vtype
#>    <int> <char> <char> <char> <num> <num>     <char>
#> 1:     1   vCap   coal  north     0   Inf   positive
#> 2:     7   vGen   coal  north     0   Inf   positive
#> 3:    13  vCost   <NA>   <NA>  -Inf   Inf continuous
lp$objective_symbol
#> [1] "vCost"

row_lo/row_up and col_lo/col_up hold the bounds; an equality row has both equal, a <= row has -Inf below. Before solving a large model, check_matrix_numbers() reports the magnitude spectrum of the coefficients, right-hand sides and bounds. Coefficients spanning more than about eight orders of magnitude, or infinite entries, are the usual cause of a solver reporting “unbounded” or “infeasible” for a model that is neither, and the offenders_* tables name the equations and variables responsible.

cm <- check_matrix_numbers(lp)
#>    section entries zeros nonfinite min_abs max_abs orders below_small
#>    COLUMNS      29     0         0    0.25     120    2.7           0
#>  OBJECTIVE       1     0         0    1.00       1    0.0           0
#>        RHS      10     8         0  600.00    1000    0.2           0
#>     BOUNDS       0     0         0      NA      NA     NA           0
#>  above_large
#>            0
#>            0
#>            0
#>            0
names(cm)
#>  [1] "summary"           "decades"           "offenders_row"    
#>  [4] "offenders_col"     "nonfinite_row"     "nonfinite_col"    
#>  [7] "structure"         "empty_col_symbols" "empty_row_symbols"
#> [10] "small"             "large"

solve_highs() passes the arrays to the HiGHS solver in the ‘highs’ package. attach = FALSE returns the result as a list rather than storing it in the model.

r <- solve_highs(toy, attach = FALSE)
r$objective
#> [1] 198000
r$status_message
#> [1] "Optimal"

status is HiGHS’s model-status code and status_message its name; 7 is “Optimal”. The primal table is the column index with the solution and the reduced cost added, the dual table the row index with the row activity and the marginal. Here the marginal on eqDemand is the cost of one more unit of demand in each region:

r$primal[r$primal$value > 0, c("symbol", "i1", "i2", "value", "reduced_cost")]
#>    symbol     i1     i2       value reduced_cost
#>    <char> <char> <char>       <num>        <num>
#> 1:   vCap   wind  north   1111.1111            0
#> 2:   vCap   coal  south    666.6667            0
#> 3:   vGen   wind  north   1000.0000            0
#> 4:   vGen   coal  south    600.0000            0
#> 5:  vCost   <NA>   <NA> 198000.0000            0
r$dual[r$dual$symbol == "eqDemand", c("symbol", "i1", "value", "marginal")]
#>      symbol     i1 value marginal
#>      <char> <char> <num>    <num>
#> 1: eqDemand  north  1000 100.0000
#> 2: eqDemand  south   600 163.3333

The arrays can also leave R: write_mps() writes them as an MPS file for any solver that reads one, and solve_mps() solves such a file locally with HiGHS and writes a solution file read_mps_solution() understands. mm_session() keeps the assembled matrix between repeated solves of the same structure with changed data.

Generating code

The file routes render the model in another language and leave the solve to that language’s toolchain. MathProg is the one to read first: the whole generated model fits on a screen, and the other two backends differ from it in ways that are easier to see once this one is understood.

MathProg, in full 

f <- write_gmpl(toy, model_dir = ws)
mod <- readLines(f$model)
cat(mod[1:grep("^solve;", mod)], sep = "\n")
#> # Model: toy
#> # two-region capacity expansion toy model
#> 
#> set tech;  # generation technologies
#> set region;  # model regions
#> 
#> 
#> set _IF_;  # Singleton set for GAMS $ operator emulation
#> 
#> set mTR dimen 2;  # technology x region pairs
#> set mR dimen 1;  # regions
#> 
#> param pCapCost{tech};  # annualised capacity cost, EUR/kW
#> param pVarCost{tech};  # variable cost, EUR/MWh
#> param pAvail{tech,region};  # availability factor
#> param pDemand{region};  # annual demand, MWh
#> 
#> var vCap{t in tech, r in region} >= 0;  # installed capacity, kW
#> var vGen{t in tech, r in region} >= 0;  # generation, MWh
#> 
#> minimize vCost: sum{t in tech, r in region} (pCapCost[t] * vCap[t,r] + pVarCost[t] * vGen[t,r]);
#> 
#> # generation is limited by available capacity
#> s.t. eqCapLim{(h,r) in mTR}: vGen[h,r] <= pAvail[h,r] * vCap[h,r];
#> 
#> # demand is met in every region
#> s.t. eqDemand{r in mR}: sum{t in tech} vGen[t,r] >= pDemand[r];
#> 
#> 
#> solve;

Reading top to bottom:

  • Sets are declared without members, mappings as sets of tuples with their dimension (dimen 2). Members and tuples come from the data file.
  • _IF_ is a one-element set multimod uses to express GAMS-style $ conditions as MathProg set filters; the toy has no conditions, so it is declared and not used.
  • Parameters are declared with their index sets only; values come from the data file.
  • Variables are declared over the full set product with iterator names taken from the model’s index aliases (t, r). Equations are declared over their domain mapping, {(h,r) in mTR}, with the iterator names the equation itself carries. This is where the domain shows up in generated code: a tuple absent from mTR yields no constraint.
  • The objective equation eqCost is not written as a constraint. The objective statement takes its right-hand side, because toy$objectives names eqCost as the equation defining vCost.

After solve; the file continues with printf statements, in two groups. The first writes constraint_stats.csv and variable_stats.csv, one line per equation and variable with the number of instances. The second writes the solution: one CSV per variable with the index columns and the value, filtered to non-zero entries, plus a log. These files are what solve_gmpl() reads back.

cat(mod[grep("^printf \"tech,region,value", mod)[1] + 0:3], sep = "\n")
#> printf "tech,region,value\n" > "solution/vCap.csv";
#> for{t in tech, r in region : vCap[t,r] <> 0} {
#>   printf "%s,%s,%f\n", t,r,vCap[t,r] >> "solution/vCap.csv";
#> }

The data file is a MathProg data section:

dat <- readLines(f$data)
cat(dat[grep("^param pAvail", dat) + 0:7], sep = "\n")
#> param pAvail default 0 := 
#> [coal,north] 0.84999999999999998
#> [gas,north] 0.84999999999999998
#> [wind,north] 0.90000000000000002
#> [coal,south] 0.90000000000000002
#> [gas,south] 0.34999999999999998
#> [wind,south] 0.25;

Two rules of the format matter when a model misbehaves. MathProg has no implicit default: a parameter referenced for a tuple that is not in the data is an error unless the declaration carries default, so every parameter is written with one (the model’s defVal, else 0). And every declared set, mapping and parameter must appear in the data section even when it is empty, so an empty mapping is written as set name := ;. A model whose data lives on disk is written one parameter at a time, so the data file for a large model never requires the whole model in memory.

JuMP

write_jump() writes two files. model.jl holds the declarations and the constraints; data.jl loads the data from the workspace at run time, so data can change without regenerating the model.

jl <- write_jump(toy, model_dir = ws)
cat(grep("^@variable|^@objective", jl, value = TRUE), sep = "\n")
#> @variable(model, vCap[mTR] >= 0)  # installed capacity, kW
#> @variable(model, vGen[mTR] >= 0)  # generation, MWh
#> @objective(model, Min, sum(get(pCapCost, h, pCapCostDef) * vCap[(h, r)] + get(pVarCost, h, pVarCostDef) * vGen[(h, r)] for h in tech, r in region))
i <- grep("eqCapLim\\[", jl)[1]
cat(jl[(i - 2):(i + 2)], sep = "\n")
#> _t0 = time()
#> # generation is limited by available capacity
#> @constraint(
#>     model,
#>     eqCapLim[(h, r) in mTR],
#>     vGen[(h, r)] <= get(pAvail, (h, r), pAvailDef) * vCap[(h, r)]
#> )
#> _log_constraint(constraint_stats, "eqCapLim", eqCapLim, length(eqCapLim), time() - _t0)

Three choices in this code are worth knowing about:

  • Variables are indexed by their domain mapping, vCap[mTR], and constraints iterate over it, eqCapLim[(h, r) in mTR]. The mapping is loaded as a Julia Set of tuples (or of strings when it has one dimension), so membership tests are constant time.
  • Parameters are dictionaries read through get() with a default, get(pCapCost, h, pCapCostDef). A tuple missing from the data yields the declared default rather than an error, which mirrors the GAMS semantics the AST follows.
  • Every constraint block is timed and counted. The generated code writes constraint_stats.csv (instances, dimension, size of the domain mapping, build time, non-zeros per row) and variable_stats.csv (instances, bound types). On a translated model these two files are the first thing to read: an equation with zero instances or a variable with no finite bound is visible there before any solve.

data.jl finds the workspace relative to its own location and detects the format from format.txt, so the same file works for CSV, Arrow IPC and Parquet workspaces. With data_mode = "embedded" the data is written into the Julia source instead, which makes a model file that runs anywhere but has to be regenerated when the data changes.

Pyomo

write_pyomo() also writes two files, model.py and data.py. The model is a Pyomo AbstractModel: declarations only, instantiated with data by data.py at run time.

py <- write_pyomo(toy, model_dir = ws, export_vars = TRUE)
mp <- readLines(py)
cat(grep("^model\\.(tech|mTR|pAvail|vGen|eqCapLim) ", mp, value = TRUE), sep = "\n")
#> model.tech = Set(doc="generation technologies")
#> model.mTR = Set(dimen=2, doc="technology x region pairs")
#> model.pAvail = Param(model.tech, model.region, default=0, domain=Reals, doc="availability factor")
#> model.vGen = Var(model.mTR, within=NonNegativeReals, bounds=(0, None))  # generation, MWh
#> model.eqCapLim = Constraint(model.tech, model.region, rule=_eqCapLim_rule)

Sets and parameters are declared with their index sets and defaults; variables over their domain mapping; constraints through a rule function per equation. The runner at the end of model.py builds the instance, picks the solver named in the PYOMO_SOLVER environment variable (set by solve_pyomo(solver = )), solves, and writes solution/status.json. With export_vars = TRUE it also writes solution/variables.json, which is what load_results reads.

Running the code

Each solve_*() function runs the toolchain on the workspace and returns a list with success, objective, status, timing, the raw solver output, and, when a model is passed, the model with solutions attached under $model.

g <- solve_gmpl(toy, ws, verbose = FALSE)
g$objective
#> [1] 198000
g$status
#> [1] "OPTIMAL"
j <- solve_jump(toy, ws, verbose = FALSE)
#> Loading solutions from: solvers/jump/solution
j$objective
#> [1] 198000
j$status
#> [1] "OPTIMAL"
p <- solve_pyomo(toy, ws, solver = "highs", verbose = FALSE, load_results = TRUE)
p$objective
#> [1] 198000
p$status$termination
#> [1] "optimal"

What each one runs, which is also how to run the code by hand from the backend’s directory when something needs a closer look:

Route Command Leaves behind in solvers/<backend>/
GLPK glpsol -m model.mod -d data.dat -o solution.sol --log solver.log solution.sol, solver.log, solution/*.csv, the two stats files
JuMP julia model.jl solution/*.csv, the two stats files, the Julia output
Pyomo python model.py solution/status.json, solution/variables.json

The first Julia run installs the packages the model needs and compiles them, which takes minutes; later runs take seconds. solve_jump() and solve_gmpl() accept timeout =; solve_pyomo() checks the Python environment with mm_check_python() before running unless ensure_env = FALSE.

Results back in R

With load_results = TRUE (the default when a model is passed) every route stores each variable’s values as a data frame under model$variables[[name]]$solution, with the dimension names as columns and value last, and copies the files to variables/ in the workspace.

g$model$variables$vGen$solution
#>   tech region value
#> 1 coal  south   600
#> 2 wind  north  1000
g$model$solution_metadata$variables_loaded
#> [1] "vCap"  "vCost" "vGen"

Because every table has the same shape, results from different routes line up directly. The objective is the simplest comparison:

objectives <- c(highs = r$objective)
if (has_glpsol) objectives["gmpl"]  <- g$objective
if (has_julia)  objectives["jump"]  <- j$objective
if (has_python) objectives["pyomo"] <- p$objective
objectives
#>  highs   gmpl   jump  pyomo 
#> 198000 198000 198000 198000

and one variable across routes is a merge on the index columns:

v_highs <- r$primal[r$primal$symbol == "vGen", c("i1", "i2", "value")]
names(v_highs) <- c("tech", "region", "highs")
v_gmpl <- g$model$variables$vGen$solution
names(v_gmpl)[3] <- "gmpl"
merge(v_highs, v_gmpl, all = TRUE)
#> Key: <tech, region>
#>      tech region highs  gmpl
#>    <char> <char> <num> <num>
#> 1:   coal  north     0    NA
#> 2:   coal  south   600   600
#> 3:    gas  north     0    NA
#> 4:    gas  south     0    NA
#> 5:   wind  north  1000  1000
#> 6:   wind  south     0    NA

The GLPK table lists only non-zero entries (the generated printf loop filters them), so the merge fills the zeros with NA; the matrix route reports every column.

When routes disagree

Same model, same data, different objective: the translation has read something differently. The cases below account for nearly all of them, in the order to check.

  1. An equation produces no rows. Its domain mapping has no tuples, or the tuples do not match the data. In R, table(lp$row_index$symbol) shows the row count per equation, and model_to_lp(on_empty_row = ) decides whether an empty row is an error (the default for user constraints), a warning or ignored. In JuMP, constraint_stats.csv shows count 0; in MathProg the same file shows the cardinality product, which is only an upper bound.
  2. A parameter’s default differs. The matrix route and JuMP use the declared defVal for a tuple missing from the data; MathProg uses the default written in the data file, which is defVal or 0. A parameter whose defVal is NULL and whose data is incomplete is read as 0 by every route, which may not be what the model meant. validate() lists parameters without data.
  3. Infinite values. Inf in parameter data cannot enter a matrix. The matrix route drops the affected rows and maps an infinite default to 0, as the energyRt writers do; MathProg receives 1e20 (write_gmpl(INF = )); JuMP and Pyomo receive Inf as a bound where the value is a bound and as a coefficient otherwise, where the solver decides. Search the data for Inf before comparing.
  4. Missing index aliases. The text backends write iterator names from the model’s index aliases. A model built in R has none until add_index_aliases() adds them; without them a sum{} is written with no iterator and glpsol rejects the file. has_index_aliases() tells.
  5. Row counts, not objectives. When the objectives differ, compare per-equation instance counts first (table(lp$row_index$symbol) against constraint_stats.csv), then per-variable bounds (lp$col_index against variable_stats.csv). A count that differs points at the equation; an objective that differs points nowhere.

Choosing a route

Route Needs Returns Use when
solve_highs() the ‘highs’ R package primal, duals, reduced costs, the LP arrays the model fits in memory and you want duals or repeated solves (mm_session())
write_mps() nothing an MPS file the solver is elsewhere, including cloud hardware
solve_gmpl() glpsol primal values a small or medium LP, or when a readable model file is the point
solve_jump() Julia primal values, build statistics a large model, or a solver only JuMP wraps (optimizer =)
solve_pyomo() Python with pyomo primal values, status the results continue in a Python pipeline
write_gams() GAMS elsewhere GAMS source hand-over to a GAMS installation or NEOS

Whatever the route, the same model object, data and workspace are behind it, which is what makes the comparison in the previous section possible.
